assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recognition that cells organise their interior through liquid-liquid phase separation into condensates (P granules and nucleoli as liquid droplets) is a simple, general mechanism behind a messy multi-scale problem, and it brings non-equilibrium statistical physics (active droplets, chemically driven phase separation) into cell biology. Originality and impact are high: the idea reorganised a large field and created a new quantitative physics of living matter.
assessment.attribution: The 2009 P-granule experiments (Brangwynne, Hyman) are the decisive discovery. Jülicher and colleagues supplied the physical theory of active droplets. A three-way prize of two experimentalists and one theorist is plausible, but others in the credited field, e.g. Rosen and Rosen-Reddy-type biochemistry, are not on the supplied list and the credit boundary is contested.
assessment.maturity: Roughly 15 years of independent confirmation and a vast follow-up literature. Quantitative theory is maturing. Timing is reasonable, though the physics-versus-chemistry/medicine boundary is a real issue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as physics rather than biology or chemistry.
Debate in the literature on how many in-cell condensates are true equilibrium liquids and how functionally relevant phase separation is.
Allocation of credit between experiment and theory and among early contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phases show that geometry and topology of parameter space have physical consequences. This is a universal mechanism that underlies Hall quantisation, topological band theory, polarisation and molecular dynamics. The originality is high and the clarity of the idea is exceptional, in the spirit of foundational papers that contain almost everything.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959; Ehrenberg-Siday earlier) and Berry (1984; with Simon's holonomy interpretation) are two distinct discoveries, each with a clear lead author. The supplied two-person configuration is workable, but it compounds two different contributions, and priority issues (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Bohm's co-authorship) are not resolved by the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: decades of experimental confirmation (Tonomura, interferometry, geometric phases in optics and NMR). If anything recognition is late.
uncertainties: Bohm is not on the credited list, so the Aharonov-Bohm credit is incomplete.
Whether the committee views this as foundational quantum physics or as a theoretical-concept prize with weak invention content.
My recollection of the priority history (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam) is from memory and unverified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is a controlled, conceptually clean framework (exact in infinite dimensions) for strongly correlated electrons. It supplies the standard description of the Mott transition and, combined with ab initio methods, of real correlated materials. This is analytic theory with a clear mechanism that has been checked against experiment.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) found the infinite-dimension limit; Georges and Kotliar (1992) mapped it to a quantum impurity problem; Müller-Hartmann also contributed early. The supplied triple is a defensible configuration, but Metzner is absent from the list and the ordering of contributions is debated.
assessment.maturity: More than 30 years of use, with cold-atom and spectroscopic confirmation of the Mott physics. Strongly mature, if possibly too methodological for some members.
uncertainties: Metzner and Müller-Hartmann priority is not represented in the supplied credit.
Quantitative accuracy for realistic low-dimensional systems remains limited and the theory is approximate in finite dimensions.
Whether theory-method prizes are favoured over discovery prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The cavity method and message passing, applied to random constraint-satisfaction problems, found glassy phase transitions in computational hardness and gave survey propagation as a new algorithm. This is statistical physics of disordered systems producing a general mechanism that connects computer science, inference and learning. Its link to the 2021 spin-glass prize (Parisi) is both an asset and a limitation.
assessment.attribution: Mézard and Parisi introduced the cavity method for spin glasses (1986), and Parisi is already a laureate. Mézard-Zecchina (2002) applied it to random K-SAT, with Mézard-Parisi-Zecchina as the key paper. A two-person prize is clean, but the work is largely an extension of a prize-winning framework, and Monasson and others also contributed to the K-SAT phase picture.
assessment.maturity: Mature in physics, with rigorous confirmation (Ding-Sly-Sun on the K-SAT threshold) and wide influence, though practical algorithm impact is mixed.
uncertainties: Whether this is sufficiently distinct from the work recognised in 2021.
Rigorous results confirm the threshold but only partly the full replica-symmetry-breaking picture.
Credit shared with Monasson and Parisi, who are not on the supplied list or already recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theory of defect-mediated melting in two dimensions with the prediction of the hexatic phase is a clean statistical-physics mechanism (dislocation and disclination unbinding, universal exponents) that is analysable and tested by simulation and colloid experiments. It extends the topological-defect framework honoured in 2016.
assessment.attribution: Kosterlitz and Thouless are already laureates (2016), so the remaining decisive contributors are Halperin and Nelson (1978) and Young (1979). The supplied triple fits, though Young's role is somewhat smaller than that of the first two.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, confirmed in colloidal and other experiments and numerics, though the nature of the 2D melting transition (first-order versus KTHNY) varies by system. Recognition could be seen as a follow-up to 2016.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees it as already covered by the 2016 prize.
Mixed experimental and numerical verdict on whether the KTHNY scenario holds in all systems.
Relative credit of Young versus Halperin and Nelson.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened a field of tunable correlated matter. The mechanism (moiré flat bands) is simple and general, and its impact is large.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald 2011 theory and the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero experiments are the decisive pair, which supports a theory-plus-experiment prize. Cao et al. and Yankowitz or Dean-group contributions are not on the credited list, so credit among experimentalists is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Strong replication across many groups within about eight years. The interpretation of the superconductivity and of the correlated phases is still unsettled, which argues for waiting.
uncertainties: The nature of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is not agreed.
Experimental credit beyond one lead author is unclear.
Maturity is limited by the age of the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, with the observation of helical edge transport in HgTe quantum wells, opened the study of topological quantum matter. The theoretical idea is clean and general, and the experimental confirmation was direct.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele (2005) made the core theory proposal, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (2006) predicted the HgTe case, and Molenkamp's group observed it (2007). Hasan's ARPES work on 3D topological insulators is a separate part of the story. Because Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not on the credited list, the allocation of the 2D case remains unresolved, and the 2016 prize (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) covers part of the conceptual territory.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with extensive confirmation in 2D and 3D, though practical applications remain limited.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize.
Missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the supplied credit.
Whether a three-person prize should cover the 2D and 3D parts together.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices are an analogue quantum simulator for Hubbard-type models, with realisation of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and later single-site resolved studies. It is a bridge between many-body theory and experiment in the spirit of statistical physics.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch-Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation (1998), and Greiner-Bloch (2002) observed the Mott transition. Hänsch and Esslinger are also credited in some accounts. The five-name credit makes allocation awkward, but a three-person prize is possible. Zoller also appears in other candidates, so overlap needs managing.
assessment.maturity: Mature for bosonic Mott physics, but fermionic Hubbard simulations are still unfinished, so part of the claim is premature.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit with trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates through Zoller and Cirac.
Whether quantum simulation is regarded as a discovery or as a technique.
Open questions on whether fermionic simulations reach the interesting low-temperature regimes.
